target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove scheduling barriers and make voting easier for workers, especially low-income workers.
objection: A federal holiday would not require private employers to give paid time off, so many retail, food service, and gig workers could still have to work or lose wages; therefore the holiday would not reliably remove the voting barrier for the people most affected.

target: AG1’s claim that a national holiday is a practical way to increase turnout.
objection: An Election Day holiday by itself is not a proven or especially effective turnout strategy compared with other reforms that directly reduce voting obstacles, such as time-to-vote laws, early/absentee/mail voting, registration reforms, and automatic voter registration.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is weak because it won’t guarantee paid time off and won’t reliably benefit low-wage workers.
objection: Even without a paid-leave mandate, a holiday changes real-world logistics: more businesses close or reduce hours, public institutions and childcare arrangements are more available, and employers are less likely to make workers choose between wages and voting, so the benefit is not limited to explicit paid leave.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday is not useful if it must be paired with other reforms.
objection: A national holiday is not meant to be the only reform; it can work alongside access measures like early voting and easier registration while directly reducing the standard work/school scheduling conflict on Election Day itself.

target: AG1’s response that holiday logistics changes will help low-income workers.
objection: Retail, service, and other lower-wage jobs often still operate on holidays, so many low-income workers can still be scheduled to work and face the same wages-versus-voting tradeoff; the holiday does not reliably solve their problem.

target: AG1’s assumption that a holiday reduces the need to request time off.
objection: For low-income workers, the real bottleneck is not just inconvenience but whether they can vote without losing income; a holiday may help workers with more flexibility while leaving retail/service workers still working or taking unpaid time.

target: AG1’s idea that a holiday can simply be added to other reforms without issue.
objection: Because an Election Day holiday is not a dependable, targeted fix, it is better to pursue direct state-level time-to-vote protections and low-friction registration or voting reforms instead of relying on uncertain employer and operational behavior.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday only matters if it guarantees paid leave.
objection: A holiday changes schedules in advance even without paid-leave rules: shifts are often reduced or rearranged, schools and daycare follow holiday schedules, and voting becomes easier during the day because it no longer collides as strongly with rigid routines.

target: AG2’s objection that low-income workers may still be scheduled and lose wages.
objection: The holiday can be paired with time-to-vote protections so workers are not forced into a wages-versus-voting tradeoff; the wage issue is an implementation concern, not a reason to reject the holiday itself.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday-related schedule changes will reliably help low-income workers.
objection: A federal holiday does not obligate private employers to provide paid time or stop scheduling workers, so it still fails to show that the holiday will reliably prevent lost wages for the workers most constrained by them.

target: AG1’s suggestion that the holiday can just be paired with time-to-vote protections.
objection: If the real fix is enforceable time-to-vote rules, then the holiday becomes an extra, costly, and uncertain layer rather than the main solution; the direct reforms alone are the reliable path.

target: AG2’s claim that time-to-vote rules make the holiday redundant.
objection: The holiday and time-to-vote protections address different parts of the problem: time-to-vote rules address wage loss, while the holiday reduces how much time people need by changing the surrounding work/school schedule and making voting easier within the day.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is ineffective because employers may ignore it.
objection: A national holiday still matters because it establishes a common public baseline across institutions like schools, public services, and civic routines, and unlike variable state rules it is uniform nationwide.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday meaningfully reduces friction around Election Day.
objection: Even if it reduces some friction, the decisive barrier is whether workers can vote without losing pay; without enforceable wage protections, the holiday remains an unreliable and inequitable lever compared with direct access reforms.

target: AG1’s argument that a holiday is additive rather than substitutive.
objection: A holiday can misallocate political effort because policymakers may treat the calendar change as the solution while the real constraint—paid time to vote and wage loss protection—remains governed by patchy state law.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday could distract from better reforms.
objection: A holiday does not have to replace targeted reforms; it can be enacted as part of a broader package and reduces reliance on those reforms by changing the baseline scheduling environment nationwide.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday is just symbolic and should be avoided because of diversion concerns.
objection: Calling the holiday misallocated assumes lawmakers will stop pursuing other reforms, but a national holiday can be pursued alongside time-to-vote rules and other access measures.

target: AG1’s claim that a nationwide calendar change helps low-income families.
objection: For many low-income parents, a holiday can create new costs: if schools or daycare close while employers still require coverage, they may face a new wages-versus-childcare tradeoff or lose voting time anyway.

target: AG1’s suggestion that the holiday can be an additive reform.
objection: In practice, once Election Day becomes a holiday, lawmakers and employers may treat the problem as solved, even though enforceable wage protections and time-to-vote guarantees remain uneven.

target: AG2’s childcare-cost objection to the holiday.
objection: The childcare concern does not defeat the holiday because the core barrier is forced schedule conflict, and the policy can be designed with enforceable time-to-vote rules that prevent wage loss while the holiday reduces the scheduling clash.

target: AG1’s claim that pairing the holiday with time-to-vote protections solves the problem.
objection: That concession shows the holiday alone is not a reliable or equitable solution; if time-to-vote protections are needed to make the policy fair, then those protections—not the holiday—are doing the important work.

target: AG1’s proposal to spend political effort on a national holiday.
objection: Passing a national holiday would require major federal legislation and political capital that could crowd out faster, more enforceable reforms like paid or protected time to vote and automatic or low-friction registration.

target: AG1’s broader claim that the holiday is a useful turnout reform.
objection: Research indicates that an Election Day holiday by itself does not outperform other voting-access reforms, so investing political effort in it is a lower-leverage choice.

target: AG1’s argument that the holiday provides a predictable nationwide baseline for planning.
objection: Even with a predictable date, the holiday is mostly duplicative if enforceable time-to-vote protections are still needed, because those protections are what actually determine whether workers can vote without losing income.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday has independent value beyond wage protections.
objection: The holiday still carries political and administrative costs and can crowd out the targeted, enforceable reforms that directly address the constraint, so its marginal benefit is too uncertain to justify it as a priority.
